goals: Compute a posterior probability from base rate and test accuracy
why: Spam filters, medical diagnosis, fraud alerts and Bayesian A/B testing all update beliefs with evidence. Ignoring base rates leads to badly wrong decisions.
explain: Bayes' theorem tells you how to **update a belief** when new evidence arrives: **posterior ∝ likelihood × prior**.

The **prior** is what you believed before (1% of transactions are fraud). The **likelihood** is how probable the evidence is under each hypothesis (an alert fires for 99% of frauds but also for 5% of normal transactions).
The **posterior** is the updated belief: given that the alert fired, how likely is fraud?
The famous surprise: when the base rate is low, even an accurate test produces mostly false alarms. That is the **base-rate fallacy**.

formula.plain: Belief in H after seeing evidence E = how well H explains E × prior belief in H, normalised.

example.title: A positive medical test
steps: Out of 10,000 people: 100 sick → 99 test positive
example.result: A "99% accurate" test gives only a 17% chance of disease after one positive result. Confirmatory tests exist for exactly this reason.

mistakes: Confusing P(positive | sick) with P(sick | positive).
takeaways: Low base rates → many false positives
Think in natural frequencies (out of 10,000 people)

practice.code:
prior, sens, fpr = 0.01, 0.99, 0.05
p_pos = sens * prior + fpr * (1 - prior)
print(round(sens * prior / p_pos, 3))      # 0.167

check.q: Base rate 0.1%, test sensitivity 100%, false-positive rate 1%. After a positive test, P(condition) is roughly…
check.why: Out of 100,000: 100 true positives vs ~1,000 false positives → about 9%.

options: The belief before seeing the evidence
